BESS Scheduling Pipeline Implementation¶

Welcome to the implementation notebook for the BESS scheduling pipeline developed for the thesis:

Robust Trading Strategy for Battery Energy Storage System in the Czech Electricity Market

The main goal of this thesis was to create a complete pipeline that generates a daily operating schedule for a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) participating in the Czech electricity market.

This notebook shows the technical implementation of the whole process, including:

  • loading and preprocessing market and weather data,
  • creating features for electricity price forecasting,
  • training point and interval forecasting models,
  • generating BESS schedules using different strategies,
  • evaluating the realized profit of each schedule.

The figure below shows the overall design of the implemented scheduling pipelines.

Select Data Interval¶

In this step, the time interval for the experiment is selected. The loaded data will later be used for feature engineering, model training, forecasting, and schedule evaluation.

The variables below define:

  • START and END - the full data range loaded from the data source,
  • TEST_START and TEST_END - the testing period used for evaluating the forecasting models and BESS schedules.

The figure below shows the time split used for the benchmark results.

After the interval is selected, the market data are loaded using the get_data function. At this stage, the dataframe contains only the original market-related signals, before additional engineered features are created.

In [24]:
START = "2024-01-01"
END = "2025-09-01"
TEST_START = "2025-06-30"
TEST_END = "2025-09-01"
df = get_data(START,END)

Feature Engineering¶

In this step, additional information is added to each timestamp in the dataset. These engineered features help the forecasting models capture patterns that are not directly visible from the raw market data.

The added features include, for example:

  • historical price information from previous days,
  • calendar features such as hour, day of week, and month,
  • seasonal features,
  • cyclic time features.
In [25]:
price_features_df = price_features(df[PRICE_COL])
df_extra_features = pd.concat([df, price_features_df], axis=1)
df_extra_features = df_extra_features.dropna().copy()
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = data_split(df_extra_features, TEST_START, TEST_END)

Model Training and Price Forecasting¶

In this step, several forecasting models are trained and used to predict electricity prices for the testing period.

The selected models are:

  • Linear Regression,
  • Random Forest,
  • CatBoost,
  • XGBoost,
  • HGBR,
  • FourCatBoost.

The parameter alpha defines the level for prediction intervals. Here, alpha = 0.05, which corresponds to a 95% confidence level.

In this first experiment, each model is trained only once on the training data. After that, it is used to forecast the whole testing period. The models are not retrained when new true prices from the testing period become available.

The function fit_and_predict trains the selected model. For models that support direct quantile prediction, the function also trains additional quantile models to create the prediction interval. So this funiton returns a dataframe with three columns:

  • y_pred -- point forecast,
  • pi_lo -- lower prediction interval bound,
  • pi_hi -- upper prediction interval bound.
In [26]:
alpha = 0.05

Forecast Evaluation¶

After the models are trained, their forecasts are evaluated using both point forecasting metrics and prediction interval metrics.

For point forecasts, the following metrics are used:

Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) RMSE measures the average size of the prediction error and gives higher weight to larger errors.

$$ RMSE = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}(y_t - \hat{y}_t)^2} $$

Mean Absolute Error (MAE) MAE measures the average absolute difference between the true and predicted prices.

$$ MAE = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}|y_t - \hat{y}_t| $$

Coefficient of Determination ($R^2$) $R^2$ shows how much of the variability in the true prices is explained by the model.

$$ R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{N}(y_t - \hat{y}_t)^2} {\sum_{t=1}^{N}(y_t - \bar{y})^2} $$

Weighted Mean Absolute Percentage Error (wMAPE) wMAPE measures the absolute forecasting error relative to the total absolute value of the true prices.

$$ wMAPE = 100 \cdot \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{N}|y_t - \hat{y}_t|} {\sum_{t=1}^{N}|y_t|} $$

For prediction intervals, the following metrics are used:

Coverage Coverage measures how often the true price lies inside the predicted interval.

$$ Coverage = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N} \mathbf{1}\left(y_t^L \leq y_t \leq y_t^U\right) $$

Average Width Width measures the average size of the prediction interval. Narrower intervals are better, but only if the required coverage is still achieved.

$$ Width = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}(y_t^U - y_t^L) $$

Winkler Score The Winkler score evaluates both interval width and missed observations. Lower values are better.

$$ W_t = \begin{cases} y_t^U - y_t^L, & \text{if } y_t^L \leq y_t \leq y_t^U, \\ (y_t^U - y_t^L) + \frac{2}{\alpha}(y_t^L - y_t), & \text{if } y_t < y_t^L, \\ (y_t^U - y_t^L) + \frac{2}{\alpha}(y_t - y_t^U), & \text{if } y_t > y_t^U. \end{cases} $$

$$ Winkler = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N} W_t $$

Here, $y_t$ is the true electricity price, $\hat{y}_t$ is the predicted price, $y_t^L$ and $y_t^U$ are the lower and upper prediction interval bounds, and $\alpha$ is the miscoverage level.

Schedule Optimization¶

Before creating the BESS schedules, the technical parameters of the battery must be defined. The same configuration is used for all scheduling strategies, so the comparison between methods is fair. The selected BESS parameters are shown in the table below.

In [29]:
cfg = BESSConfig()

Deterministic Schedule Optimization¶

After the price forecast is created, the next step is to find the best possible BESS schedule for the forecasted prices.

The schedule is created using a mixed-integer linear programming model. The optimizer decides how much energy should be charged or discharged in each 15-minute interval.

Variables and parameters used in the model:

  • $t$ - index of the 15-minute interval,
  • $T$ - number of intervals in one day,
  • $\hat{y}_t$ - forecasted electricity price in interval $t$,
  • $c_t$ - charged energy in interval $t$,
  • $d_t$ - discharged energy in interval $t$,
  • $SOC_t$ - state of charge of the battery in interval $t$,
  • $z_t$ - binary variable that decides whether the battery is charging or discharging,
  • $\eta^{ch}$ - charging efficiency,
  • $\eta^{dis}$ - discharging efficiency,
  • $\bar{E}$ - maximum battery capacity,
  • $\bar{C}$ - maximum charge per interval,
  • $\bar{D}$ - maximum discharge per interval,
  • $E^{init}$ - initial state of charge,
  • $E^{final}$ - final state of charge,
  • $N^{cyc}$ - maximum number of equivalent cycles per day,
  • $cost^{deg}$ - degradation or throughput cost.

The optimization model is:

$$ \max \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \left( \hat{y}_t d_t - \hat{y}_t c_t - cost^{deg}(c_t+d_t) \right) $$

subject to:

$$ SOC_{t+1}=SOC_t+\eta^{ch}c_t-\frac{d_t}{\eta^{dis}} $$

$$ 0 \leq SOC_t \leq \bar{E} $$

$$ SOC_0 = E^{init} , SOC_T = E^{final} $$

$$ 0 \leq c_t \leq \bar{C} z_t , 0 \leq d_t \leq \bar{D}(1-z_t) $$

$$ \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} c_t \leq N^{cyc}\bar{E} , \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} d_t \leq N^{cyc}\bar{E} $$

$$ z_t \in \{0,1\} $$

True Optimal Schedule¶

To compare the forecast-based schedules, we also create a schedule using the true electricity prices from the testing period.

This schedule is not realistic in practice, because true future prices are not known when the BESS schedule has to be created. However, it is useful as a benchmark, because it shows the best possible profit that could be achieved with the selected BESS parameters.

This schedule is called the true optimal schedule or perfect-foresight schedule.

In [31]:
schedule_true = solve_price_by_day(y_test, cfg)
print("True profit:", realized_profit_from_schedule(schedule_true,y_test, cfg))
all_model_schedules.update({"True schedule":schedule_true})

True profit: 662215.5524584487

Peak-Hour Baseline Schedule¶

As a simple baseline for comparison, a fixed peak-hour schedule is created.

In this schedule, the battery is charged during two predefined low-price periods:

  • 02:00--03:45,
  • 13:00--14:45.

The battery is then discharged during two expected peak-price periods:

  • 05:00--06:45,
  • 16:00--17:45.

This baseline does not use any price forecast or optimization. It only follows a fixed daily rule based on the typical structure of electricity prices. forecast-based schedules.

In [32]:
schedule_peak_hours = make_peak_hours_schedule(X_test.index,cfg)
print("Peak hours profit:", realized_profit_from_schedule(schedule_peak_hours,y_test, cfg))
all_model_schedules.update({"Schedule Peak hours":schedule_peak_hours})

Peak hours profit: 354823.5

Yesterday-Optimal Baseline Schedule¶

The second baseline uses information from the previous day.

For each testing day, the best schedule is first created using the true prices from the previous day. These prices are already known when the schedule for the next day has to be prepared. The same schedule is then reused for the current day. It assumes that the price pattern today will be similar to the price pattern from yesterday.

This approach does not require a price forecasting model, but it still uses the optimization model to create the schedule from yesterday's known prices.

In [33]:
schedule_yesterday = make_yesterday_schedule(y_test.index,df[PRICE_COL],cfg)
print("Yesterday optimal profit:", realized_profit_from_schedule(schedule_yesterday,y_test, cfg))
all_model_schedules.update({"Schedule yesterday optimal schedule":schedule_yesterday})

Yesterday optimal profit: 567326.2928220221

Realized Profit Evaluation¶

The final step of the pipeline is to evaluate the created BESS schedules on the true electricity prices from the testing period.

For each schedule, the following values are calculated:

  • Profit - realized profit obtained by applying the schedule to the true market prices.
  • Profit loss - difference between the perfect-foresight profit and the profit of the evaluated schedule.
  • Average daily loss - average profit loss per day.
  • Match rate - percentage of time intervals where the evaluated schedule selected the same action as the perfect-foresight schedule.
  • EUR/MW/year - estimated annual profit normalized by the BESS power capacity.

This evaluation connects the forecasting part with the final business objective: creating a schedule that produces the highest realized profit.

Results¶

The previous cells explained all important parts of the BESS scheduling pipeline. To make the final experiments easier to run, these steps are now wrapped into several helper functions:

  • run_forecast_pipeline -- trains forecasting models and creates price forecasts,
  • run_schedule_pipeline -- creates deterministic predict-then-optimize schedules,
  • run_schedule_robust_pipeline_mc -- creates robust schedules using Monte Carlo scenarios,
  • run_schedule_robust_pipeline_bootstrap -- creates robust schedules using bootstrap scenarios.

The following cells use these functions to reproduce the main summer experiment from the thesis.

In [35]:
import pandas as pd
def run_forecast_pipeline(df: pd.DataFrame, models: list[str],alpha: float,update: bool = False):
    forecast_dict = {}
    X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = data_split(df, TEST_START, TEST_END)
    for model_name in models:
        if update:
            result_df = fit_and_predict_update(model_name,X_train,y_train,X_test,y_test,alpha)
        else:
            result_df = fit_and_predict(model_name,X_train,y_train,X_test,alpha)
        forecast_dict[model_name] = result_df
        print(f"{model_name} forecast finished")
    return forecast_dict

def run_schedule_pipeline(forecast_dict: dict[str, pd.DataFrame],cfg: BESSConfig):
    schedule_dict = {}
    for model_name, forecast_df in forecast_dict.items():
        schedule = solve_price_by_day(forecast_df["y_pred"], cfg)
        schedule_dict[model_name] = schedule
        print(f"{model_name} schedule finished")
    return schedule_dict

def run_schedule_robust_pipeline_mc(forecast_dict: dict[str, pd.DataFrame],cfg: BESSConfig):
    schedule_dict = {}
    for model_name, forecast_df in forecast_dict.items():
        scenarios = mc_scenarios (forecast_df, alpha,n_scenarios=1000,clip_to_interval=False)
        schedule = solve_scenarios_by_day(scenarios, cfg)
        schedule_dict[model_name] = schedule
        print(f"{model_name} schedule finished")
    return schedule_dict

def run_schedule_robust_pipeline_bootstrap(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    models: list[str],
    cfg: BESSConfig,
    alpha: float,
    residual_days: int = 30,
    n_scenarios: int = 100,
    update: bool = False,
):
    df = df.sort_index().copy()
    X_train_full, X_test, y_train_full, y_test = data_split(df, TEST_START, TEST_END)

    train_days = pd.Index(X_train_full.index.normalize().unique()).sort_values()

    resid_days = train_days[-residual_days:]

    mask_resid = X_train_full.index.normalize().isin(resid_days)
    mask_train = ~mask_resid

    X_resid = X_train_full.loc[mask_resid].copy()
    y_resid = y_train_full.loc[mask_resid].copy()

    X_train = X_train_full.loc[mask_train].copy()
    y_train = y_train_full.loc[mask_train].copy()

    print("=" * 80)
    def print_split_info(name: str, X: pd.DataFrame):
        if len(X) == 0:
            print(f"{name}: EMPTY")
        else:
            print(
                f"{name}: {X.index.min()} -> {X.index.max()} | "
                f"rows={len(X)} | days={X.index.normalize().nunique()}"
            )
    print_split_info("TRAIN", X_train)
    print_split_info("RESID", X_resid)
    print_split_info("TEST ", X_test)
    print("=" * 80)

    forecast_dict = {}
    scenario_dict = {}
    residual_library_dict = {}
    for model_name in models:

        if update:
            resid_forecast = fit_and_predict_update(model_name,X_train,y_train,X_resid,y_resid,alpha)
        else:
            resid_forecast = fit_and_predict(model_name,X_train,y_train,X_resid,alpha)

        if resid_forecast is None:
            continue

        residual_library = build_daily_residual_library(y_resid, resid_forecast["y_pred"],steps_per_day=96)
        residual_library_dict[model_name] = residual_library

        if update:
            forecast_df = fit_and_predict_update(model_name,X_train,y_train,X_test,y_test,alpha)
        else:
            forecast_df = fit_and_predict(model_name,X_train,y_train,X_test,alpha)

        forecast_dict[model_name] = forecast_df
        print(f"{model_name} forecast finished")

        scenarios_df = bootstrap_scenarios_by_day_df(forecast_df,residual_library, n_scenarios,RANDOM_STATE)
        scenario_dict[model_name] = scenarios_df

        schedule_dict[model_name] = solve_scenarios_by_day(scenarios_df, cfg)
        print(f"{model_name} schedule finished")

    return forecast_dict, schedule_dict, scenario_dict

Robust Schedule Optimization¶

In the robust scheduling approach, the schedule is not created from only one forecasted price path. Instead, multiple possible future price scenarios are generated from the prediction intervals.

Each scenario represents one possible development of electricity prices during the next day. The optimizer then searches for one BESS schedule that performs well across all generated scenarios.

To make the schedule less sensitive to bad scenarios, the robust method uses Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR). CVaR focuses on the worst part of the scenario outcomes. In this context, it penalizes schedules that could lead to large losses or low profit in unfavorable price scenarios.

In [44]:

Bootstrap Robust Scheduling¶

This cell runs the robust scheduling pipeline using bootstrap scenario generation.

Only the FourCatBoost model is used here, because it was one of the best performing forecasting models in the previous experiments. The function first creates forecasts, then builds a residual library from the last 90 historical days, and finally generates 500 bootstrap price scenarios for each testing day.

These scenarios are used to create a robust BESS schedule. The schedule is then evaluated against the true prices and compared with the perfect-foresight schedule.

In [49]:
models = ["FourCatBoost"]
if scenario_dict is None:
    forecast_dict, schedule_dict, scenario_dict = run_schedule_robust_pipeline_bootstrap(df_extra_features,models,cfg,alpha,
    residual_days=90, n_scenarios=500,update=True)
schedule_bootstrap = solve_scenarios_by_day(scenario_dict["MAPIE-FourCatBoost"],cfg)

Example Schedule¶

The next plot shows one example of a BESS schedule created by two methods:

  • predict-then-optimize,
  • robust scheduling.

It is only a visual example of how the created schedules can look.

In [53]:
timeIndex = pd.date_range(start="2025-07-25",freq="15min",periods=96,tz="UTC")

plot_schedule_comparison_2x2(
schedule_dict["OLS"].loc[timeIndex],
schedule_dict["MAPIE-FourCatBoost"].loc[timeIndex],
schedule_true.loc[timeIndex],
schedule_peak_hours.loc[timeIndex],
cfg,
"Predict-then-optimize vs Robust schedule comparison")
In [54]:
robust_average_schedule = average_schedule(schedule_dict["MAPIE-FourCatBoost"],timeIndex)
predict_optimaze_average_schedule = average_schedule(schedule_dict["OLS"],timeIndex)
true_average_schedule = average_schedule(schedule_true,timeIndex)
naive_average_schedule = average_schedule(schedule_peak_hours,timeIndex)

Average Schedule Comparison¶

The next plot shows the average charging and discharging behavior for both methods compared with the true optimal schedule.

This helps to see when the battery is usually charged or discharged during the day and how close the created schedules are to the best possible schedule.

In [55]:
plot_schedule_comparison_2x2(
robust_average_schedule,
predict_optimaze_average_schedule,
true_average_schedule,
naive_average_schedule,
cfg,
"Predict-then-optimize vs Robust schedule comparison",)
